newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Thyssen unit refocuses, profit falls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thyssen unit refocuses, profit falls.

text.p: Thyssen Industrie AG annnounced on Monday a 37.5 percent drop in 1995-96 profits to 65 million marks ($39.9 million) and said it would refocus on auto parts, lifts and factory equipment to boost profits and sales.

Last year's results were hurt mainly by massive losses at shipbuilding subsidiary Blohm & Voss and in warehouse equipment, leading to drastic cutbacks in those areas, chairman Eckhard Rohkamm told reporters.

Lifts remained Thyssen Industrie's most profitable business, but the company made money on all its operations except Thyssen Henschel and shipbuilding, which took 91 million marks in extraordinary write-downs.

The company, which is the capital goods unit of Thyssen AG, said it designated other divisions for restructuring which could be potential core areas along with auto parts, lifts and machine tools. They include Thyssen Polymer, Thyssen Wharves and the plant construction unit Thyssen Anlagentechnik.

The company planned to shed non-core activities including weapons systems and locomotives with sales totalling one billion marks, he said. The 3,000 to 3,500 jobs in these areas would not be eliminated, but would continue under new management, he said.
"The world is changing, and enterprises must change with it," Rohkamm said. "Our 1995-96 results did not fulfil our plans and expectations."
Sales in the year ended September 30 totalled 9.147 billion marks, up from 8.497 billion, while orders on hand reached 10.671 billion marks, up from 9.922 billion marks.
Rohkamm said the company aimed to boost income from ordinary business to 250 million marks in the current year and 350 million marks next year. Income was 239 million marks last year.

The unit would aim for a return on sales of four to five percent. Its 19.3 percent return on equity was already well above the Thyssen Group's goal of 12.5 percent, but Thyssen Industrie would aim for 30 percent next year.
Thyssen Industrie expected to boost sales in its Thyssen Budd Automotive unit to six billion marks by the year 2000 from 4.9 billion in 1995-96, he said.
The auto parts division showed a profit of 155 million marks last year, up from 113 million the year before.
The lift division saw sales of four to six billion marks by 2000, up from 2.9 billion in 1995-96. It showed a profit of 121 million marks last year, down from 166 million the year before.

The third core division, machine-tool maker Thyssen Production Systems, would aim to boost sales to two billion marks from last year's 1.2 billion. Its 1995/96 profit was 26 million marks, turning around from a loss of seven million the year before.

Rohkamm said the company, which through its Thyssen Henschel unit is the leading industrial partner developing the Transrapid magnetic levitation train, was awaiting a government study due at the end of March with fresh forecasts about the financial viability of the planned Hamburg-Berlin route.
Thyssen has invested 130 million marks in the high-tech high-speed train.
